assignments.title: 3.1 VR Assignment — Hypothesis Hub
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · THE GOOD LIFE EXPERIMENT
3.1 VR Assignment — Hypothesis Hub (Project Stage 1 of 9)

Objective: Set up your VR research lab and stock it with your starting hypotheses. Apply what you learned about Explanation Freeze (Lesson 1) by generating at least three hypotheses about what will happen in your Good Life Experiment — not just one.

This is the first stage of the persistent Good Life Experiment lab you'll build across Module 3. You'll return to this space every VR session for the rest of the module.

What you'll build

  1. Pick your lab space. Choose any environment that feels like a research space to you — a science lab, a study, an observatory, a treehouse, a cozy library, whatever fits how YOU work. This is the space you'll return to every VR session in Module 3.
  2. Designate the Hypothesis Hub area. Pick one wall or one corner of your lab to be the "Hypothesis Hub." Place a whiteboard there as the centerpiece.
  3. Post your primary hypothesis. On a sticky note, write the prediction you genuinely think is most likely: "When I do [my chosen experiment], I think [this] will happen." Place it on the Whiteboard.
  4. Generate at least two alternatives. Apply the Lesson 1 thaw process. What ELSE could happen? Maybe nothing measurable. Maybe the opposite of what you predicted. Maybe something you didn't see coming. Add a sticky note for each.
  5. Tag each hypothesis with a likelihood. Next to each sticky note, write or attach the rating: Very likely, Somewhat likely, or Unlikely.
  6. Snapshot the hub. Step back. Take a snapshot that captures all your hypotheses and their likelihood tags.
  7. Record a video. Walk us through your hypotheses out loud: what you predicted, what the alternatives are, why you weighted them the way you did.

Why this matters

In Lesson 1 you learned that locking onto a single explanation is the enemy of clear thinking. Real scientists don't just write down what they hope will happen — they list out what could happen and weigh the possibilities. Doing this BEFORE the experiment is how you avoid fooling yourself once data starts coming in. The hub you build today is the foundation of your whole lab.

Submit

  1. The snapshot of your Hypothesis Hub (named Lastname_HypothesisHub_MJCRT).
  2. The recorded video walking through your three or more hypotheses and their likelihoods.

Download both and upload here in Canvas.

assignments.title: Assignment 1: Thawing Explanation Freeze
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
Assignment 1: Thawing Explanation Freeze

In today's lesson you learned that Explanation Freeze happens when your brain locks onto the first explanation it finds and stops looking for others. This assignment gives you practice thawing that freeze using real moments from your own life.

  1. Think of three recent situations where you jumped to a conclusion about what was really going on.
  2. For each of the three situations, write down:
    • The situation itself.
    • Your initial explanation — the one your brain froze on first.
    • At least three different alternative explanations you didn't consider at the time.
    • The real answer, if you ever found out what actually happened.

Remember, the goal isn't to prove your first guess was wrong — it's to practice generating other possibilities before you settle on one.

assignments.title: 3.2 VR Assignment — Scientific Predecessors
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · THE GOOD LIFE EXPERIMENT
3.2 VR Assignment — Scientific Predecessors (Project Stage 2 of 9)

Objective: Apply the Semmelweis lesson to your own experiment. Add a "Predecessor Wall" to your VR research lab, and use it to refine the hypotheses you posted in Stage 1.

Return to the lab space you set up in Stage 1. You'll add a new section and update the existing Hypothesis Hub.

What to do

  1. Return to your VR research lab. Open the same space you used for Stage 1 (your Hypothesis Hub should still be there).
  2. Designate a "Predecessor Wall" area. Pick a new wall or corner of the lab. Place a whiteboard there.
  3. Add Semmelweis as your first predecessor. On a sticky note, write a one-sentence summary of his story: he was stuck on the wrong popular theories about childbed fever, then noticed something nobody else was looking at — doctors not washing their hands. Add it to the Predecessor Wall.
  4. Walk back to your Hypothesis Hub from Stage 1. Look at what you posted there a week ago.
  5. Ask Semmelweis's question of yourself: "What's the 'handwashing' explanation I might be unfairly dismissing for MY experiment?" Add at least one new sticky-note hypothesis to your hub — something you didn't take seriously the first time.
  6. Tag it with a likelihood (Very likely / Somewhat likely / Unlikely) like the others.
  7. Snapshot both the new Predecessor Wall and your updated Hypothesis Hub.
  8. Record a video walking us through what changed and why. Talk about what Semmelweis's case taught you about your own thinking.

Why this matters

Stage 1 was the first pass: you wrote down the hypotheses that occurred to you naturally. The thing about Explanation Freeze is that it doesn't feel like you're stuck — the obvious explanations feel obvious. Semmelweis's story shows what it actually takes to break out: noticing the thing nobody else is looking at. Stage 2 forces you to ask, before your data starts coming in, whether you're already locked in.

Submit

  1. A snapshot of your new Predecessor Wall.
  2. A snapshot of your updated Hypothesis Hub (showing the new hypothesis you added).
  3. The recorded video explaining what changed in your thinking.

assignments.title: 3.3 VR Assignment — Methodology Wall
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · THE GOOD LIFE EXPERIMENT
3.3 VR Assignment — Methodology Wall (Project Stage 3 of 9)

Objective: Design HOW you'll actually run your Good Life Experiment. Apply the four-step scientific reasoning cycle from Lesson 3 to plan your daily action, your measurements, your duration, and what would prove your hypothesis WRONG.

Return to the lab space you've been building in Stages 1 and 2. You'll add the Methodology Wall, which is the part of the lab your future self will check every day.

What to do

  1. Return to your VR research lab. Pick a new wall — this is the Methodology Wall. Place a whiteboard there.
  2. Post your final research question. On a sticky note at the top, write the one-sentence question your experiment answers (the research question from the Module 3 project intro page that matched your chosen experiment).
  3. The daily action. Sticky note: what exact behavior you'll do every day for the experiment. Be specific: "Spend 20 minutes outside, between 4 PM and 6 PM" beats "spend time outside."
  4. What you'll measure. Sticky note: name the variable you'll track in your Excel log. Two is fine, three is plenty — pick measurements that match your research question (mood 1–10, focus 1–10, hours of sleep, did the habit Y/N).
  5. Duration. Sticky note: how many days the experiment runs. Most of the project assumes ~14 days — long enough to see a pattern, short enough to finish before the capstone.
  6. Your negative test. Sticky note: what observation, if it happened, would prove your top hypothesis WRONG? This is the most important card on the wall. Without it, you're just confirming what you already believe.
  7. Snapshot the entire Methodology Wall.
  8. Record a video walking through each sticky note. Out loud, name: research question, daily action, measurements, duration, negative test.

Why this matters

Without a written methodology, you'll let yourself off the hook when the experiment gets hard. With one, you know exactly what to do tomorrow, the next day, and the day after. The negative-test sticky note is what separates a real experiment from a confirmation hunt. Lock it in now, before any data comes in.

Submit

  1. A snapshot of your Methodology Wall (all sticky notes visible).
  2. The recorded video walking through your plan.

assignments.title: 3.4 VR Assignment — Confidence Scale
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · THE GOOD LIFE EXPERIMENT
3.4 VR Assignment — Confidence Scale (Project Stage 4 of 9)

Objective: Lock in your starting credence in your Good Life Experiment hypothesis. Apply graded belief from Lesson 4: instead of "I think this will work" or "I think this won't," pick a percentage and defend it.

Return to your VR research lab. You'll add a long Confidence Scale to a wall and place a marker on it.

What to do

  1. Return to your VR research lab. Pick a long wall — one you can stand back from and see end-to-end.
  2. Build the Confidence Scale. Use a long whiteboard or a row of sticky notes laid out left to right. Mark labels at the ends and the middle:
    • Left end: 0% — definitely false
    • Middle: 50% — no idea
    • Right end: 100% — definitely true
    Add tick marks at 25%, 75%, etc., for reference.
  3. Restate your top hypothesis on a sticky note. (From your Hypothesis Hub: the prediction you think is most likely.)
  4. Place the sticky note on the scale at your honest starting credence. Don't round to 100% or 0% — almost nothing in real life is at the extremes.
  5. Defend the number. Add a second sticky note next to the first explaining WHY you picked that credence. What experience, evidence, or reasoning supports it?
  6. Snapshot the Confidence Scale with your marker placed.
  7. Record a video walking to your marker, pointing to where you put it, and reading both sticky notes aloud. State the percentage clearly — you'll be checking this in Stage 8.

Why this matters

The number you place today is what your data will either confirm, raise, or lower over the course of the experiment. Without a starting credence, there's nothing to update against — you just end up "feeling like" your hypothesis was right. With a number, you can actually measure how your thinking changed.

  2. The recorded video walking through your number and your reasoning.

assignments.title: 3.5 VR Assignment — Data Collection Station
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · THE GOOD LIFE EXPERIMENT
3.5 VR Assignment — Data Collection Station (Project Stage 5 of 9)

Objective: Set up the part of your VR lab where your incoming data will live. Daily Excel entries begin today — your VR station is the visual home for the patterns that emerge.

Return to your VR research lab. You'll add the Data Collection Station and start the daily habit of logging.

What to do

  1. Return to your VR research lab. Pick a new wall for the Data Collection Station — ideally near your Methodology Wall so you can glance from one to the other.
  2. Build the empty board. Place a whiteboard and divide it into a few labeled zones with sticky notes:
    • "Daily Entries" (left side — this is where you'll post screenshots of your Excel log)
    • "Early Patterns" (middle — sticky notes you'll add as patterns emerge)
    • "Things I Didn't Expect" (right side — surprises)
  3. Open your Excel data log. Today, log Day 1 of your experiment in Excel:
    • Today's date in column A.
    • Did you do the habit? Y/N.
    • Your two measurements.
    • One sentence of notes.
  4. Screenshot your Day 1 Excel entry. Upload it into your VR space.
  5. In VR, place that screenshot in the "Daily Entries" zone of your Data Collection Station.
  6. Commit to the routine. Add a sticky note above the board with your daily entry time: "I'll log every day at [time]." Be specific. Before bed works for most people.
  7. Snapshot the Data Collection Station with Day 1 posted.
  8. Record a video walking through your station and explaining how you'll use it across the coming days.

Why this matters

Most experiments fail not because the hypothesis is wrong but because the experimenter doesn't actually collect the data. The single most important thing you can do for your project is establish the daily logging routine. The VR station gives you a visible, physical reminder that this is real research. Don't skip a day.

  2. The recorded video walking through your station and committing to the daily routine.

M/J CRITICAL THINKING
Assignment 5: Calibrating Degrees of Belief

For each of the following statements, do two things:

A. Briefly describe all the background knowledge you have at your disposal related to the statement.
B. Using the red-marble method, determine your credence in the statement.

Red-marble method refresher

  • Using the number of red marbles to estimate the strength of your belief in a statement, how many red marbles are needed to be indifferent between the statement's truth and the chance of pulling a red marble from a bag mixed with red and blue marbles (nbr of blue = 100 − nbr of red)?
    • If you prefer the marble bet, adjust the number of red marbles DOWN.
    • If you prefer the statement bet, adjust the number of red marbles UP.

  8. You will be alive in 50 years

assignments.title: 3.6 VR Assignment — Evidence Library
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · THE GOOD LIFE EXPERIMENT
3.6 VR Assignment — Evidence Library (Project Stage 6 of 9)

Objective: Decide BEFORE you collect more data what counts as evidence in your experiment. Define a positive result, a negative result, and an ambiguous result — in your own words — so future-you can't move the goalposts when the data comes in.

Return to your VR lab space. You'll add the Evidence Library, the part of your lab where you've decided in advance what each kind of outcome means.

Why a library, and why now

Lesson 6 made the case that evidence usually supports or undermines a claim — rarely proves it. If you wait until your data is in to decide what counts as supporting or undermining, you'll unconsciously stretch your interpretation toward what you already believed. Defining your evidence categories now, while you still have a clean view, is what makes the experiment honest.

What to do

  1. Return to your VR research lab. Pick a new wall or shelf area — this is your Evidence Library.
  2. Place a whiteboard labeled "Evidence Library." Place three smaller whiteboards (or 3 zones on one wide whiteboard) next to it, labeled:
    • Supports my hypothesis
    • Undermines my hypothesis
    • Ambiguous — doesn't tell me either way
  3. For each of the three zones, post 2–3 sticky notes with specific examples that would belong there. Be concrete — use the variable you're actually measuring in your data log.
    • Example (Supports): "Avg sleep quality goes from 5 to 7+ over 14 days" or "Mood at 7+ on at least 9 of 14 days."
    • Example (Undermines): "Avg sleep quality stays at 5 or drops" or "Mood at 7+ on fewer than 5 of 14 days."
    • Example (Ambiguous): "Big spikes and dips, no clear pattern" or "Improvement only on weekends — could be the habit, could be weekends."
  4. Add one "decoy" sticky note to the Supports zone, then move it to the Ambiguous zone (or remove it). What did you almost count as supporting that probably shouldn't count? Write that on a separate sticky and explain in one line.
  5. Snapshot the entire Evidence Library.
  6. Record a video walking through each zone. Read one example from each category out loud.

A note on honesty

The "decoy" step matters. The most common mistake in real research isn't bad math — it's quietly redefining what counted as success after the data came in. By locking in your categories now, with examples you can point to, you protect the integrity of your experiment from future-you.

Submit

  1. A snapshot of your Evidence Library (all three zones visible with sticky notes).
  2. The recorded video walking through your evidence categories.

assignments.title: Assignment 6: The Missing Cookie Jar
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · MODULE 3 · ASSIGNMENT 6
The Missing Cookie Jar
Evaluate evidence in a real (fictional) mystery.

Evaluate the Case of the Missing Cookie Jar

Detectives, you have been called in to solve a perplexing mystery. A cookie jar has gone missing from the school kitchen, and several pieces of evidence have surfaced. Your job is to evaluate the evidence, determine how it supports or undermines different suspects, and decide who the most likely culprit is.

Instructions

  1. Read the crime story below. Pay close attention to the details of the case and the evidence provided.
  2. Evaluate each piece of evidence. For each item, explain whether it supports or undermines the claim that a specific suspect is guilty.
  3. Analyze the case as a whole. Based on the evidence, write a paragraph explaining who you believe is the most likely suspect and why.
  4. Consider counterarguments. Is there any evidence that makes you less confident in your conclusion?

The Story: The Case of the Missing Cookie Jar

It was a quiet afternoon at Jefferson Middle School — until it wasn't. Mr. Jenkins, the school's janitor, burst into the teachers' lounge, exclaiming, "The cookie jar from the kitchen is gone!" This wasn't just any cookie jar; it belonged to Mrs. Patton, the head of the kitchen staff, and it was her pride and joy. The jar always sat on the countertop, filled with cookies for staff meetings.

The crime had occurred during the lunch break, between 12:00 and 12:30 PM. Three suspects quickly emerged:

SuspectProfile
A — AlexAn 8th grader with a known sweet tooth. Alex had been seen loitering around the kitchen earlier that day.
B — BenjiA 7th grader who had been caught sneaking snacks from the kitchen before.
C — CathyA 6th grader who was delivering notes to teachers during the lunch break.

Evidence found during the investigation

  1. Evidence #1: Cookie crumbs were discovered on Alex's desk in the science lab, where Alex had been during lunch.
  2. Evidence #2: A teacher reported seeing Benji near the kitchen door around 12:15 PM, carrying what looked like a cloth bag.
  3. Evidence #3: Security footage shows Cathy walking past the kitchen with an empty backpack at 12:10 PM and returning past the same area at 12:25 PM, with the backpack appearing full.
  4. Evidence #4: The cookie jar lid was found on the ground near the science lab, where Alex had been during lunch.
  5. Evidence #5: Multiple witnesses reported seeing Benji playing soccer on the field at 12:20 PM, far from the kitchen.
  6. Evidence #6: Mrs. Patton, the head of the kitchen staff, recalled Cathy visiting the kitchen earlier that day and asking, "What kind of cookies are in there today?" Cathy quickly left when another teacher entered the room.

Your task

For each piece of evidence (1 through 6):

  • Identify which suspect it supports or undermines.
  • Explain your reasoning clearly — remember, evidence usually shifts confidence rather than proving things outright.

Then, write a paragraph summarizing who you think is the most likely culprit and why. Be sure to address any evidence that weakens your conclusion or leaves room for doubt.

Good luck, Detective! We're counting on you to crack this case.

A Word document (uploaded via the OneDrive tab) containing:

  1. Your six evidence evaluations — one paragraph each (supports/undermines which suspect, and why).
  2. Your conclusion paragraph — who you think did it AND what evidence weakens your case.

assignments.title: 3.7 VR Assignment — Mid-Experiment Audit
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · THE GOOD LIFE EXPERIMENT
3.7 VR Assignment — Mid-Experiment Audit (Project Stage 7 of 9)

Objective: Apply the Question of Evidence (QoE) to your real, in-progress experiment. Look at your data so far — not at the end — and ask honestly: how strongly does this evidence support or undermine your hypothesis?

Return to your VR lab. You've been collecting data in your Excel log for at least a week by now. The Mid-Experiment Audit is where the lab becomes a real science lab and not a wish-fulfillment lab.

Before you enter VR

Open your Excel data log. Quick check:

  • How many days of data do you have? (Aim for at least 7 before doing this audit.)
  • Compute a simple summary: average of your main measurement, and how many days hit your "positive result" criterion from the Evidence Library.
  • Take a screenshot of the data and have it on your phone or a second window. You'll bring it into VR.

What to do in VR

  1. Return to your VR lab and find a clean wall. Add a whiteboard labeled "Mid-Experiment Audit."
  2. Place your data screenshot. Upload your screenshot file as an image and pin it to the audit wall. This is the actual evidence you're evaluating.
  3. Three sticky notes for the three QoE steps:
    • Step 1 sticky: "If my hypothesis is TRUE, how likely is what I'm seeing in this data?" Estimate: high / medium / low. Explain in one sentence.
    • Step 2 sticky: "If my hypothesis is FALSE, how likely is what I'm seeing in this data?" Estimate: high / medium / low. Explain in one sentence.
    • Step 3 sticky: "Compare." Which estimate is higher? By how much?
  4. Conclusion sticky. Where does your current evidence land on the strength scale — strongly supports, weakly supports, neutral, undermines, strongly undermines? Write the verdict.
  5. Two "alternative explanations" sticky notes. Name two OTHER reasons (besides your hypothesis) that could explain your data so far. (Examples: it was a weird week, you also changed something else, the measurement isn't capturing what you think it's capturing.)
  6. Decision sticky. Based on this audit, what do you do for the rest of the experiment? Three options:
    • Keep going exactly as planned.
    • Adjust something (specify what — e.g., add a measurement, change when you do the habit, log more details).
    • Stop and reset (rare, only if something is fundamentally broken).
  7. Snapshot the entire Mid-Experiment Audit wall.
  8. Record a video walking through your audit. Out loud: read the data summary, the three QoE steps, the strength verdict, the alternative explanations, and your decision for the remaining days.

Honesty note

The whole point of doing this AT THE MIDDLE of your experiment, not the end, is that the conclusion isn't locked in yet. If your evidence so far is "weakly supports" or even "neutral," say so. Real scientists do mid-experiment audits all the time and adjust accordingly. Cherry-picking only the data that supports your starting hypothesis isn't research — it's confirmation.

M/J CRITICAL THINKING · MODULE 3 · ASSIGNMENT 7
Evaluating Evidence
Apply the Question of Evidence (QoE) to three scenarios.

Practice analyzing evidence using the Question of Evidence (QoE) by comparing competing theories and determining how strongly the evidence supports or contradicts each theory.

Instructions

For each of the three scenarios below:

  1. Identify the competing theories.
  2. Examine the provided piece of evidence.
  3. Answer the three sub-steps of the QoE:
    • Step 1: How likely is this evidence if Theory A is true?
    • Step 2: How likely is this evidence if Theory B is true?
    • Step 3: Compare the likelihoods. How much more likely is the evidence under one theory than the other?
  4. Conclude which theory the evidence supports (or undermines) and how strongly.

Scenario 1 — Exercise and Mood

  • Theory A: Regular exercise improves mood.
  • Theory B: Mood is unrelated to exercise.
  • Evidence: After a week of daily exercise, someone reports feeling happier.

Scenario 2 — Eating Breakfast and Focus

  • Theory A: Eating breakfast improves focus during school.
  • Theory B: Focus during school is unrelated to eating breakfast.
  • Evidence: A student who normally skips breakfast eats breakfast for a week and reports feeling more focused during morning classes.

Scenario 3 — Pet Ownership and Stress

  • Theory A: Having a pet reduces stress levels.
  • Theory B: Stress levels are unrelated to pet ownership.
  • Evidence: A new pet owner reports feeling significantly less stressed two months after adopting their pet.

Repeat the process for all three scenarios. Make reasonable estimates for the likelihoods (you won't have exact numbers — that's fine; aim for "a lot more likely," "a bit more likely," "about the same"). Explain your reasoning in each step — the explanation is the point of the assignment.

3.8 VR Assignment — Belief-Update Timeline (Project Stage 8 of 9)

Objective: Make your belief shift visible. In your VR lab, build a Belief-Update Timeline showing your starting credence, your mid-experiment audit, and your final credence after all the data is in. This is the Bayesian view of your own experiment.

You should have ~14 days of data by now. Finish your data log before entering VR for this stage. Take a final screenshot of the completed log.

Before you enter VR

  • Open your Excel log. Compute a final summary (average of your main measurement; total "positive result" days vs. total days).
  • Look back at your Stage 4 Confidence Scale notes: what was your starting credence in your hypothesis? (Red-marble language: "very sure," "sure," "unsure," etc., or a number like 7/10.)
  • Look at your Stage 7 Mid-Experiment Audit: where did you land then?
  • Now decide your final credence in your hypothesis based on the full dataset.

What to do in VR

  1. Return to your VR lab. Find a long wall (or use 3 whiteboards in a row). Place a whiteboard labeled "Belief-Update Timeline."
  2. Build three columns on the wall:
    • Column 1: BEFORE (your starting credence from Stage 4)
    • Column 2: MID-EXPERIMENT (your audit credence from Stage 7)
    • Column 3: AFTER (your final credence now)
  3. For each column, post these three sticky notes:
    • Credence (red-marble language OR a number out of 10)
    • One-sentence reason WHY that's your credence at that point
    • The strongest piece of evidence that pushed you there
  4. Place your final data screenshot on the AFTER column as an uploaded image. This is your "posterior evidence."
  5. Verdict sticky. In the AFTER column, post one large sticky note answering: did your credence MOVE between BEFORE and AFTER? In which direction, and by how much? In one sentence: was your hypothesis supported, undermined, or left unclear?
  6. Honesty sticky. Post one sticky note answering: "If my final credence didn't move much, what does that tell me — about my hypothesis, my data, or the way I measured?"
  7. Snapshot the entire Belief-Update Timeline (all three columns visible).
  8. Record a Video MyRec walking the camera left-to-right through the three columns. Read each credence and reason out loud. End at the verdict sticky.

Why this stage matters

This is the moment your experiment becomes Bayesian, not just descriptive. Anyone can collect data. The intellectual move is showing how your belief actually moved (or didn't) in response to that data. A credence that didn't move when the evidence pushed against it is the same trap Lucy fell into with her hockey jersey. A credence that flipped completely on one weak data point isn't honest either — you're chasing whatever just happened. The Timeline is the record of you doing it right.

assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · MODULE 3 · ASSIGNMENT 8
Field Biology
Use Bayesian Updating to identify a mystery animal.

You're a scientist studying a newly discovered animal, and you're trying to figure out if it's primarily a plant-eater or a meat-eater. Use the information provided to update your beliefs step by step. At each stage, calculate the new ratio and explain your reasoning.

Starting Point: Priors

You know that in the region where this animal was found, 70% of animals are plant-eaters and 30% are meat-eaters.

Starting ratio (priors):
Plant-eater : Meat-eater = 70 : 30 = 7 : 3

The Evidence

Evidence 1 — The animal has sharp teeth.

  • Sharp teeth are 3 times more likely to be found in meat-eaters than in plant-eaters.
  • Likelihood ratio for this evidence: 1 : 3 (Plant-eater : Meat-eater).

Evidence 2 — Traces of plant material are found in the animal's stomach.

  • Plant material in the stomach is 5 times more likely in plant-eaters than in meat-eaters.
  • Likelihood ratio for this evidence: 5 : 1 (Plant-eater : Meat-eater).

Evidence 3 — You observe the animal stalking another animal.

  • Stalking behavior is 4 times more likely in meat-eaters than in plant-eaters.
  • Likelihood ratio for this evidence: 1 : 4 (Plant-eater : Meat-eater).

Your task

Update your beliefs step by step. After each piece of evidence, write the new posteriors (which become the priors for the next step). Show your work, including the multiplication.

  1. After Evidence 1. Multiply priors by Likelihood Ratio 1. Write new posteriors.
  2. After Evidence 2. Use posteriors from step 1 as new priors. Multiply. Write new posteriors.
  3. After Evidence 3. Use posteriors from step 2 as new priors. Multiply. Write FINAL posteriors.

Give me your final set of posteriors and tell me: Is the animal more likely to be a plant-eater or a meat-eater?

Submit

M/J CRITICAL THINKING · THE GOOD LIFE EXPERIMENT
3.9 VR Assignment — Fallacy Audit (Project Stage 9 of 9 — final lab stage)

Objective: Audit your own Good Life Experiment for fallacies BEFORE you write up the capstone. Catch yourself before you publish — this is how real researchers protect their work from confirmation hunting.

You have a complete Belief-Update Timeline (Stage 8). Before you record your capstone tour, do one last pass: look at your data, your conclusions, and your draft of the story you're about to tell — and check whether you've snuck in any fallacies.

Before you enter VR

Open your data log, your Methodology Wall sticky notes, your Belief-Update Timeline, and a fresh document. Skim your "After" sticky and ask yourself, honestly:

  • Am I about to claim something caused something else when I might just have a coincidence? (False cause)
  • Am I dodging the disappointing data by pointing at unrelated good things? (Red herring)
  • Am I taking one good day and treating it as proof the whole experiment worked? (Decomposition or hasty generalization)

What to do in VR

  1. Return to your VR lab. Find a final wall (or area) and label it "Fallacy Audit."
  2. Three fallacy-check sticky notes. One for each common trap. On each, name one specific way you ALMOST (or DID) commit that fallacy in your experiment write-up:
    • False cause sticky: "I almost said X CAUSED Y, but actually…"
    • Red herring sticky: "I was tempted to bring up X to dodge the data on Y, but…"
    • Decomposition / hasty generalization sticky: "I was about to claim the whole experiment worked based on X, but…"
    If you genuinely didn't fall into one of these traps, write a sticky explaining what kept you out of it.
  3. Revised conclusion sticky. Write your final, audited one-sentence answer to your research question. Hedge appropriately — use red-marble language. (Examples: "I'm fairly sure that…," "I'm unsure but lean toward…," "I can't tell from this experiment whether…")
  4. "What I'd do differently" sticky. One sticky note: if you ran this experiment again, what's the ONE methodology change you'd make?
  5. Walk the whole lab. Now, with the audit done, walk your entire lab from Stage 1 (Hypothesis Hub) through Stage 8 (Belief-Update Timeline). This is your dress rehearsal for the capstone tour.
  6. Snapshot the Fallacy Audit wall.
  7. Record a Video MyRec of the audit wall AND a quick walk of the full lab in order. Out loud: name each fallacy you considered, your revised conclusion, and your one methodology change.

Why this stage matters

The most common reason real research goes wrong isn't bad math — it's an unexamined fallacy in the story the researcher tells about their results. By auditing your own work for false cause, red herring, and decomposition BEFORE you record the capstone, you're doing the exact intellectual virtue work Lesson 9 named. This is also the moment your lab becomes a portfolio piece: a complete, self-audited, honest VR research artifact.

  2. The Video MyRec: audit wall narration + walk-through of the full lab in order. (This doubles as your warm-up for the capstone.)

assignments.title: Assignment 9: Analyzing Fallacies
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · MODULE 3 · ASSIGNMENT 9
Analyzing Fallacies
Pick 3 of 10 arguments and break each one down with Bayes' Rule.

Below are 10 arguments. Choose only THREE (3). For each one you choose, follow these steps:

  1. Claim: Rewrite the claim in your own words to show what the argument is trying to say.
  2. Evidence: Identify the supposed evidence given to support the claim.
  3. Bayesian Analysis:
    • Assume the claim is TRUE — how likely is the evidence?
    • Assume the claim is FALSE — how likely is the evidence?
  4. Upshot: Explain why the evidence is (or isn't) relevant to the claim and whether the argument works or fails.

Use the example below to structure your responses. Be clear and concise.

Example Analysis (for practice)

Argument: "Why are you mad I forgot to take out the trash? Don't you remember how nice I was to you last week?"

  • Claim: It's okay that I forgot to take out the trash because I was nice to you last week.
  • Evidence: I was nice to you last week.
  • Bayesian Analysis:
    • Assume it's okay I didn't take out the trash: how likely is it that I was nice to you last week? Fairly likely — say 70%. Being nice isn't tied to forgetting chores.
    • Assume it's NOT okay I didn't take out the trash: how likely is it that I was nice to you last week? Just as likely — about 70%. Being nice and forgetting chores aren't strongly connected.
  • Upshot: Being nice last week doesn't affect whether forgetting the trash is okay. The argument fails because the evidence distracts from the real issue. (Red herring.)

Arguments — pick THREE to analyze

  1. "You don't want to go to the party? I can't believe you never want to have fun or see your friends!"
  2. "I wore my lucky socks, and we won the game. Clearly, the socks made us win."
  3. "I met one dog that barked at me, so all dogs must be mean."
  4. "You either help me with my homework, or you don't care about me at all."
  5. "If we let people chew gum in class, soon everyone will stop following any rules!"
  6. "Don't listen to Jamie's idea for the project — he never gets good grades."
  7. "Everyone else is skipping practice today, so it must be okay."
  8. "You have to let me borrow your bike; if you don't, I'll be so sad!"
  9. "I'm the leader because I'm the one in charge."
  10. "Why are you upset I didn't invite you to the party? You got invited to one last year!"

Extra Credit

Find a fallacious argument from a book, movie, or real life. Analyze it using the same 4-step method and include it in your submission.

M/J CRITICAL THINKING · MODULE 3 CAPSTONE
The Good Life Experiment
Video MyRec Tour of Your Complete VR Research Lab
Submitted via Canvas · Substantive teacher-graded assessment

This is the culminating piece of Module 3. Across nine lessons you've built a complete VR research lab and run a real 2-week behavioral experiment on yourself. Now you'll present it the way a research scientist would — as a guided tour through your lab in the structure of a research paper: Problem → Background → Methodology → Results → Analysis → Conclusion.

What you're delivering

A single Video MyRec recorded inside your VR lab. You'll walk through your lab in order, narrating each station, and present your experiment in the six sections of a research paper. Target length: 6–10 minutes. (Honest time estimate: shorter than 6 minutes is probably skipping sections; longer than 10 is probably losing the audience.)

The six sections of your tour

Map each section to a station in your VR lab. The audience should hear you transition: "Now walking to the Methodology Wall…"

1. Problem — Hypothesis Hub (Stage 1)

What to say: What question were you trying to answer? Why does it matter? Read your research question and your starting hypothesis off the Hypothesis Hub.

2. Background — Scientific Predecessors (Stage 2)

What to say: Who thought about this before you? Name 1–2 of the thinkers / studies / sources from your Scientific Predecessors wall. What did THEY find? How did that shape your prediction?

3. Methodology — Methodology Wall + Excel Log (Stages 3, 5)

What to say: Exactly what you did. Read off your Methodology Wall: daily action, measurements, duration, your negative test. Show your Excel log briefly. Mention the Evidence Library (Stage 6) — how you defined positive, negative, and ambiguous results BEFORE the data came in.

4. Results — Data Collection Station + Belief-Update Timeline (Stages 5, 8)

What to say: What did the data show? Share two numbers: your average measurement and how many days hit your "positive result" criterion. Show your data screenshot. Avoid interpretation in this section — just describe what happened.

5. Analysis — Confidence Scale + Mid-Audit + Belief-Update Timeline (Stages 4, 7, 8)

What to say: How did your credence move from BEFORE to AFTER? Apply the Question of Evidence to your own data: was the evidence more likely under your hypothesis or under the alternative? Was it strongly or weakly supportive? Mention what the Mid-Experiment Audit added.

6. Conclusion — Fallacy Audit (Stage 9)

What to say: Your final, audited answer (hedged appropriately — use red-marble language). Name one fallacy you almost committed and avoided. Name one thing you'd change if you ran this experiment again. Close with: what virtue did this project ask of you most?

Before you record — checklist

  • Lab is complete — all 9 stations visible and labeled.
  • Excel data log is finalized; final screenshot is placed in the lab (Belief-Update Timeline).
  • You've done one practice walk silently to plan the route between stations.
  • You've done one practice walk with narration to check timing (aim for ~7–8 minutes).
  • You know your starting credence, your final credence, and at least one fallacy you avoided.
  • Your verdict is hedged in red-marble language, not "I proved it" or "I disproved it."

Submit

  1. Your Video MyRec — the full 6-section guided tour, 6–10 minutes.
  2. A one-page Word document with: your research question, your final verdict (one paragraph), and your "what I'd do differently" answer (one paragraph).

Grading rubric

This is the substantive teacher-graded assignment for Module 3. Your teacher will use the rubric below in Canvas SpeedGrader.

Criterion4 — Exemplary3 — Proficient2 — Developing1 — Beginning
Understanding of the material Tour uses Module 3 concepts (QoE, priors, posteriors, fallacies) precisely and in the right places. Uses most of the concepts correctly; one or two misapplications. Names a few concepts but misses or misuses several. Concepts barely appear or are used incorrectly.
Quality of reasoning Belief shift is honestly traced from priors through evidence to posteriors. Fallacy avoidance is genuine. Reasoning is sound; belief shift is shown; minor logical gaps. Conclusion is stated but reasoning to get there is thin or skipped. Conclusion is asserted without evidence-based reasoning.
Clarity and precision Tour is well-paced (6–10 min), clearly narrated, easy to follow station-to-station. Clear and complete; pacing or transitions are uneven. Hard to follow in places; misses one or more sections. Disorganized or significantly under length; sections missing.
Intellectual honesty Verdict is hedged in red-marble language. Names a fallacy avoided. Admits what would be changed. Hedges most claims; some honest self-critique. Overclaims results or under-acknowledges weakness. Claims to have "proved" the hypothesis or hides problems.

Why this assignment matters

You've done what very few middle schoolers ever do: you ran a real behavioral experiment on yourself for two weeks, collected data, and applied a serious framework (the Question of Evidence + Bayesian Updating) to interpret what you found. The capstone is where you tell that story like a scientist — in the same structure used in academic journals, lab reports, and conference talks. This isn't busywork. This is research practice, in VR, at thirteen years old.

M/J CRITICAL THINKING · VR RESEARCH LIBRARY PROJECT
4.5 VR Assignment — Inference Board (Project Stage 5 of 8)

Objective: For each curated source, post 1-2 sticky notes listing INFERRED claims — what's implied but not stated outright. This is the between-the-lines layer of your library.

Return to your library. The Inference Board sits next to (or beneath) the Direct Claims Board you built in Stage 4.

Before you enter VR

Re-read (or rewatch / relisten to) each source with the between-the-lines questions from Lesson 5:

  • What is the author assuming I already know?
  • What is being implied without being said?
  • What might be hidden or accidentally missing?

For each source, find 1-2 strong inferences — conclusions you can reasonably draw from the source even though the source doesn't state them directly.

What to do in VR

  1. Return to your library. Beneath each Direct Claims Board (from Stage 4), add an Inference Board.
  2. Label each Inference Board with a Whiteboard IFX titled "Between the Lines — [source name]."
  3. Post 1-2 sticky notes per source, each with one inferred claim. Use a different color or marker than your Direct Claims so they're visually distinct.
    • [ARTICLE PLACEHOLDER — Expert-to-Expert] → 1-2 inferences
    • [ARTICLE PLACEHOLDER — Expert-to-Lay] → 1-2 inferences
    • [ARTICLE PLACEHOLDER — Lay-to-Lay] → 1-2 inferences
    • [VIDEO PLACEHOLDER] → 1-2 inferences
    • [PODCAST PLACEHOLDER] → 1-2 inferences
    • [VR EXPERIENCE PLACEHOLDER] → 1-2 inferences
  4. Add an "…but also" sticky. For at least TWO sources, add an "…but also" sticky that captures something the source seems to be HIDING or hasn't mentioned. This forces you to read suspiciously, not just sympathetically.
  5. Snapshot the Inference Board across all six sources.
  6. Record a Video MyRec walking the inference boards. For each source, read your strongest inference and (where applicable) the "…but also" sticky. Note how each inference goes BEYOND what the source actually said.

Honesty check

Your inferences are YOUR moves — not the source's. Mark them clearly so future-you (and your teacher) can tell the difference between "the source said X" (Direct Claims Board) and "I think the source is implying X" (Inference Board). Conflating the two is the most common research error.

assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · VR RESEARCH LIBRARY PROJECT
4.7 VR Assignment — Connection Web (Project Stage 7 of 8)

Objective: Use the 3D pen to draw the connections between your six curated sources. Where do they agree? Where do they disagree? Where do they complete each other? This is the synthesis layer of your library — the move that turns six separate sources into one coherent body of evidence.

Return to your library. The Connection Web is the centerpiece of the room you've built. Stand in the middle of the library so you can draw lines TO each Source Shelf.

Before you enter VR

Look at your Question Wall (Stage 2), Direct Claims Board (Stage 4), and Inference Board (Stage 5) all at once. For each of your starred priority questions, ask:

  • Which sources tried to answer this question?
  • Do they agree? If yes, list the points of agreement.
  • Do they disagree? If yes, where exactly? Why?
  • Does one source COMPLETE another — filling in something the first one left out?

What to do in VR

  1. Return to your library. Find a central spot from which all six Source Shelves are visible.
  2. Place a Whiteboard IFX in the center labeled "CONNECTION WEB — SYNTHESIS."
  3. Use the 3D pen to draw connection lines from the central whiteboard to each shelf. Color/style each line by its relationship:
    • Solid green — the two sources AGREE on this point.
    • Dashed red — the two sources DISAGREE on this point.
    • Solid blue — one source COMPLETES another (fills a gap).
  4. Label each line with a small sticky note naming the specific connection ("Both say X" or "A says X; B says NOT-X" or "A misses Y; B explains it").
  5. Three Pattern Stickies on the central whiteboard:
    • "Where they all converge" — the strongest agreement across the curated set.
    • "Where they sharply disagree" — the biggest open question in the set.
    • "What's missing" — what NONE of the six sources adequately addressed.
  6. One synthesis sentence sticky. Pin one large sticky to the central whiteboard with a SINGLE SENTENCE synthesizing your topic across all six sources. This is your "what I now think" statement — the new understanding that emerged from putting it all together.
  7. Snapshot the central whiteboard with the full web visible.
  8. Record a Video MyRec — start at the central whiteboard, read your synthesis sentence, then walk a few of the connection lines (especially the disagreements) explaining what they mean.

Submit

  1. A snapshot of your Connection Web (central whiteboard + colored connection lines + pattern stickies + synthesis sentence).
  2. The Video MyRec reading your synthesis sentence and walking key connection lines.

assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · MODULE 4 CAPSTONE
Annotated Bibliography & Library Tour
The Module 4 substantive assessment
Submitted via Canvas · Teacher-graded

This is the culminating piece of Module 4. You've built a complete VR Research Library across eight stages. Now you'll deliver two things: a formal annotated bibliography document, and a polished recorded video library tour.

Part 1: The Annotated Bibliography (Word document)

For each of the 4 articles you found for your VR library, write an annotated entry. Each entry has THREE parts:

A. Citation

Title, Author/Creator, Publication Date, Link. Same format as Stage 8.

B. Summary (3-5 sentences)

In your own words, summarize the article's main argument or content. This is the SUMMARIZE skill from Lesson 7 in action. Include the article's text structure (Lesson 6) in one phrase: "uses a cause-and-effect structure to…" or "compares X and Y to argue…"

C. Evaluation (4-6 sentences)

Evaluate the article on the same four variables you used at the Source Shelves (Stage 3):

  • Audience: Who was this written for?
  • Author: Who wrote it, and what's their expertise or likely bias?
  • Purpose: Why was this written — to inform, persuade, entertain, or sell?
  • Context: When and where was it published, and what larger conversation or moment is it part of?

Four annotated entries, one for each shelf — you supply the articles you found:

  • Article 1 (straight news report)
  • Article 2 (opinion or editorial piece)
  • Article 3 (official, expert, or organizational source)
  • Article 4 (your choice — a genuinely different perspective)

End the document with one Synthesis Paragraph (5-8 sentences) drawing your overall conclusion from your whole set of articles — the move you rehearsed at the center of your Connection Web (Stage 7).

Part 2: The Library Tour (Video MyRec)

Record a polished walk through your VR library, in order from Foyer to Bibliography. Target length: 6-9 minutes. Make eight clear transitions, one per stage:

The 8 stations to narrate (in order)

  1. Library Foyer (Stage 1) — introduce your topic and why it matters.
  2. Question Wall (Stage 2) — read your 4 starred priority questions.
  3. Source Shelves (Stage 3) — introduce the six sources by type and one-line Big Picture.
  4. Direct Claims Boards (Stage 4) — point to your starred sharpest claim per source.
  5. Inference Boards (Stage 5) — mention 1-2 of your strongest between-the-lines reads.
  6. Structure Maps (Stage 6) — show the structural skeleton + key visual for one or two sources.
  7. Connection Web (Stage 7) — this is the heart of the tour. Read your one-sentence synthesis. Walk one agreement, one disagreement, one "what's missing."
  8. Bibliography (Stage 8) — close at the bibliography whiteboard. State that you've cited all six sources and that the annotated bibliography is in the accompanying Word document.

Before you submit — checklist

  • All six annotated entries follow the Citation / Summary / Evaluation format.
  • Your synthesis paragraph names at least one agreement, one disagreement, and one gap across the source set.
  • You've cited any AI assistance you used in drafting the bibliography (per Lesson 8).
  • Your library tour Video MyRec hits all eight stations in order.
  • The tour ends with your synthesis sentence — the "what I now think" line from your Connection Web.
  • Both files are saved in OneDrive and named correctly.

Submit

  1. The annotated bibliography as a Word document.
  2. The library tour Video MyRec.

This is the teacher-graded substantive assessment for Module 4. Same four criteria your teacher used in Module 3.

Criterion4 — Exemplary3 — Proficient2 — Developing1 — Beginning
Understanding of the material All six annotated entries accurately summarize and evaluate; Module 4 concepts (structure, inference, synthesis) are used precisely. Most entries summarize accurately; concepts used correctly with minor slips. Summaries are present but shallow or off-target in places. Summaries miss the main point or are copied/paraphrased weakly.
Quality of reasoning Evaluations name credibility, contribution, AND gap for each source; synthesis paragraph identifies real agreement, disagreement, and missing piece. Most evaluations cover all three dimensions; synthesis is sound. Evaluations skip a dimension; synthesis exists but is thin. Evaluations are surface-level; no real synthesis.

Citations present; minor paraphrase issues; AI use mostly acknowledged. Some citation or paraphrase issues; AI use unclear. Plagiarized passages or missing citations.

Why this assignment matters

You've just done what serious researchers do before they write a paper: built a working library, evaluated each source, mapped how they connect, and produced an annotated bibliography. This is the foundation skill that future essays, research papers, and college projects will build on. And you did it in VR — in a workspace you can revisit, expand, or hand off as a portfolio piece.

M/J CRITICAL THINKING · DISPUTATIO PROJECT
5.1 VR Assignment — Arena & Thesis (Disputatio Stage 1 of 3)

Objective: Build your VR Disputatio Arena, choose your topic from the permitted list, and post your starter thesis with supporting premises. This is the foundation of the course final.

Pick a space that feels right for a serious argument: a Greek agora, a Roman forum, a parliamentary chamber, a modern town hall, a seminar room. The setting frames your defense — pick one that means something to you and your topic.

Before you enter VR

  1. Pick your topic. Choose ONE from the permitted topics list on the Disputatio Project Intro page. Write it down.

  3. Draft your one-sentence thesis. The position you'll defend. Be specific. Not "AI is bad" — instead, "AI-generated music violates the intellectual labor of human artists." Not "Fast fashion is bad" — instead, "Fast fashion brands' rapid production cycles cause more environmental harm than their affordability justifies."

M/J CRITICAL THINKING · DISPUTATIO PROJECT
5.2 VR Assignment — Argument Map + Counterargument Wall (Disputatio Stage 2 of 3)

Objective: Make your argument's logic visible — and then build a wall of the strongest counterarguments a serious opponent could throw at you. Apply Lesson 2's three strategies (falsify, show bad support, add new info) TO YOUR OWN argument before someone else does.

Return to the Disputatio Arena you set up in Stage 1. The argument map goes near the thesis. The counterargument wall faces the thesis — this is where your opponents stand.

Before you enter VR

  1. Apply the three evaluation strategies to YOUR thesis. Ask:
    • Are any of MY premises actually wrong, or assuming something they shouldn't?
    • Is the conclusion really supported by the premises, or am I stretching?
    • What important information am I leaving OUT? What could someone bring in that would change the conclusion?
  2. Brainstorm 5+ counterarguments. Don't filter. Use AI as a sparring partner if you want — ask: "Give me the strongest counterarguments to [your thesis]." Verify any factual claims AI gives you.
  3. Pick the THREE strongest counterarguments. Not the weakest, not the most obvious. The ones that, if you're honest, actually give you pause.

What to do in VR

  1. Return to your Disputatio Arena.
  2. Build the Argument Map. Near your thesis whiteboard, use the drawing tool to draw your argument's logical structure:
    • Boxes for each premise.
    • Arrows from each premise to the conclusion (thesis).
    • If a premise depends on another premise, show that with sub-arrows.
  3. Label each premise box with a sticky note. Color them by type (deductive support vs. inductive support).
  4. Build the Counterargument Wall. Pick a wall FACING your thesis. Place a whiteboard labeled "COUNTERARGUMENTS."
  5. Post three counterargument stickies, one per strongest objection. Each sticky has:
    • The counterargument in one sentence.
    • Which strategy it uses (falsify / bad support / new info).
    • How worried YOU are about this counterargument: ⚠️ serious / ❗ manageable / ✔ minor.
  6. For your "serious" counterarguments, add a small "RESPONSE NEEDED" tag — you'll address these in Stage 3 and again in the capstone.
  7. Snapshot the arena from a vantage point where the argument map AND the counterargument wall are both visible.
  8. Record a video: stand at the thesis, walk the argument map (read each premise aloud), then turn to the counterargument wall and read the three counterarguments. End on the most serious one and say what worries you about it.

Honesty check

If all three of your counterarguments are easy for you to dismiss, you're probably picking weak ones. A serious disputatio means choosing counterarguments that actually challenge you — the ones that make you wonder if your thesis needs adjustment. That's the move scholars have done in disputatio for centuries.

Objective: Build a Fact-Check Station in your arena, verify every load-bearing claim, and refine your thesis and premises in response to the three counterarguments from Stage 2. By the end of this stage, the arena is fully built and ready for the capstone presentation.

Before you enter VR

  1. List every load-bearing claim in your premises. A claim is load-bearing if your argument FALLS APART without it being true. Examples: statistics, named studies, historical dates, quotes, "experts say X."
  2. Verify each one against a real source. For each:
    • VERIFIED: found in a credible source. Note the source.
    • UNVERIFIED: couldn't find a credible source. You'll need to either find one, drop the claim, or label it as your own opinion.
    • UNCERTAIN: found mixed evidence. Note both sides.
  3. Look at your three counterarguments from Stage 2. For each, plan a refinement:
    • Can you tighten/weaken the conclusion to dodge this counterargument?
    • Can you sharpen a premise to close off this counterargument?
    • If neither: how will you address this head-on in your presentation?

What to do in VR

  1. Return to your arena. Stand between your argument map and your counterargument wall — that's where the Fact-Check Station goes.
  2. Place a whiteboard labeled "FACT-CHECK STATION."
  3. For each load-bearing claim, post a sticky note with the claim, its verification status, and the source (if verified). Use a color code:
    • Green — VERIFIED
    • Yellow — UNCERTAIN
    • Red — UNVERIFIED
  4. Update your thesis and premises. Walk back to your thesis whiteboard. For any refinement you planned:
    • Either replace the old sticky with the refined version, OR
    • Cross out the old wording on the sticky and add a new sticky with the refined wording right next to it (clearer for the capstone tour to show the change).
  5. Counterargument responses. Walk to your counterargument wall. For each "⚠️ serious" counterargument from Stage 2, add a "RESPONSE" sticky directly underneath it with your 1-2 sentence response.
  6. Cuts list. Off to the side, post a sticky listing any UNVERIFIED claims you decided to CUT from your argument. (Cutting weak claims is a strength, not a loss.)
  7. Snapshot the whole arena. By now there's a lot in it: thesis (refined), argument map, counterargument wall (with responses), fact-check station, and cuts list.
  8. Record a video walking through the WHOLE arena in tour order: thesis → argument map → counterargument wall → fact-check station → cuts list. Total: ~4 minutes. This is your dress rehearsal for the capstone.

Why this stage matters

Stage 3 is where your disputatio becomes honest. Anyone can claim things. You're showing your work: here's what I claimed, here's where I checked it, here's what I cut because I couldn't verify it. That's the difference between a serious argument and a performance.

Submit

  1. A snapshot of the full arena (thesis + argument map + counterargument wall with responses + fact-check station + cuts list).
  2. The recorded video dress rehearsal walking the whole arena in order.

assignments.title: The Disputatio
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING · MODULE 5 CAPSTONE · COURSE FINAL
The Disputatio
Defended argument + Great Conversation timeline + Self-assessment
Submitted via Canvas · Teacher-graded

This is the culminating piece of Module 5 — and the course final project. You've built a complete VR Disputatio Arena across three stages. Now you'll deliver three things: a defended-argument document, a video presentation recorded inside your arena, and an AI Self-Assessment.

Part 1: The Defended-Argument Document (Word)

A formal write-up of your disputatio. Use these sections, in order:

A. Thesis (1 sentence)

Your refined thesis from Stage 3 — the position you're defending.

B. Why this topic (2-3 sentences)

Why this matters to you. The honest reason — not a manufactured one.

C. Premises (3-5 numbered bullets)

Each premise in one sentence with a citation to the source that supports it. Apply Module 4 citation conventions.

D. The Three Strongest Counterarguments & Your Responses

For each of the three counterarguments from Stage 2 (refined and addressed in Stage 3):

  • State the counterargument in your own words.
  • Explain why a thoughtful critic might raise it.
  • Give your response — either a refinement of your thesis, OR a head-on defense.

E. Great Conversation Map (paragraph + bullet list)

What named debates, schools of thought, or key thinkers exist around this topic? Use the AI "great conversation" method — but verify everything. Cite at least 4 distinct sources you've actually read or reviewed.

F. Fact-Check Log

Your fact-check station, written out: every load-bearing claim, status (verified / uncertain / cut), and the source you checked it against. This is the integrity layer of your disputatio.

Part 2: The Disputatio Presentation (Recorded Video)

Recorded inside your VR arena. Target length: 7-10 minutes.

The walk-through, in order

  1. Enter the arena. Briefly describe the space you chose and why.
  2. Read your thesis aloud at the thesis whiteboard.
  3. Walk the argument map. Read each premise. Show the logical structure with the drawing tool lines.
  4. Walk the counterargument wall. Read each of the three counterarguments and your response. Spend the most time on the one rated "serious."
  5. Stop at the Fact-Check Station. Point to 2-3 verified claims and 1 cut claim. Show that you've done your homework.
  6. Build the Great Conversation moment. Walk to one final wall (or use the air around your thesis) and add a timeline marker or sticky-note row naming the named thinkers / debates / schools of thought you found. Explain how YOUR thesis fits in.
  7. Defend. Restate your thesis. Acknowledge what your strongest critic would still say. Then give your final defense in 2-3 sentences.

Part 3: AI Self-Assessment (short Word document)

The reflection the revision proposal calls for — the move that distinguishes intentional users of AI from accidental dependents on it. In 3 short sections:

A. What I used AI for in this project

Be specific. Brainstorming counterarguments? Finding the great conversation? Generating a fact-check list? Drafting? Be honest.

B. What I built myself

The reading, the thinking, the structure, the writing, the verification — what did YOU do? Be specific.

C. The choice I'm making about AI

"Going forward, what do I want to become good at MYSELF? What am I comfortable depending on AI tools to help me with?" Give honest, specific answers — this is the most important part of the self-assessment.

Before you submit — checklist

  • Thesis is one sentence, refined and specific.
  • All three counterarguments are real challenges (not strawmen) and each has a real response.
  • Every load-bearing claim has a verified source — or has been cut from the argument.
  • The Great Conversation map names actual thinkers/debates you've encountered (not just AI-generated names — verified ones).
  • The AI Self-Assessment is honest about what AI did vs. what you did.
  • All three files are named correctly and saved in your OneDrive course folder.

Submit

  1. The defended-argument document (Word).
  2. The disputatio presentation (recorded video).
  3. The AI Self-Assessment (Word).

File names:
· LastName_FirstName_Disputatio_MJCRT
· LastName_FirstName_AISelfAssessment_MJCRT

📁 M365 REMINDER
Both Word documents saved to your Optima → Critical Thinking → MJCRT_2025-26 folder, submitted via the OneDrive tab. See the pinned M365 Setup & File Organization Guide.

Grading rubric

Course final project. Same four criteria your teacher has used across the course.

Criterion4 — Exemplary3 — Proficient2 — Developing1 — Beginning
Understanding of the material Concepts from all five modules show up where appropriate (argument structure, evidence evaluation, source credibility, integrity, AI literacy). Thesis is sharp. Most concepts used correctly; minor slips. Some concepts used; others missing or misapplied. Concepts barely visible; thesis vague.
Quality of reasoning Three counterarguments are genuinely strong. Responses are real (refinement or head-on). Fact-check log is complete. Logic of the argument is tight. Counterarguments serious; responses adequate; fact-check log mostly complete. Counterarguments are weak (strawmen) OR responses don't actually address them; fact-check log thin. Counterarguments missing or trivial; responses superficial; no fact-checking.
Clarity and precision Tour is well-paced (7-10 min). Document is well-organized. Presentation defends a clear position. Tour and document are clear; pacing or organization slightly uneven. Tour skips a section or runs too short/long; document is hard to follow. Tour incomplete; document disorganized; position unclear.
Intellectual honesty Every load-bearing claim verified or cut. AI use openly acknowledged and reflected on. Great Conversation map cites only verified sources. Self-assessment is specific and honest. Citations present; AI use acknowledged; minor verification gaps. Some unverified claims; AI use unclear; self-assessment shallow. Unverified claims throughout; AI use hidden or overclaimed; self-assessment generic.

Why this assignment matters

The disputatio has been a tool of serious intellectual life for nearly a thousand years — longer than the printing press, longer than universities as we know them, longer than English itself. By doing it — researched, fact-checked, defended, in a VR arena you built — you're not just finishing this course. You're stepping into a tradition that runs from medieval Paris and Oxford through every serious thinker since. That's the work.

About this module: In Module 1 you learned how to prepare like an intellectual; in Module 2 you learned how to act like one. Module 3 is the engine: you'll learn how intellectuals actually think. Across nine lessons you'll cover what to do when an explanation runs out (Lessons 1–2), how scientists actually reason (Lesson 3), how to calibrate how strongly you believe what you believe (Lessons 4–5), what counts as evidence (Lessons 6–7), how to update your beliefs in light of new evidence (Lesson 8), and how to spot bad thinking in others' work and your own (Lesson 9).
